blocks.text: The queue from the last lesson is the plain kind. You'll meet **four** kinds in total. They differ in two things: **where** items may join and leave, and **who** gets served next.

blocks.alt: Four kinds of queue. A simple queue joins at the back and leaves at the front. A circular queue is the same on a fixed ring of slots. A deque joins and leaves at both ends. A priority queue always serves the smallest (or largest) key first.

blocks.text: Join at the **back**, leave from the **front**, first in, first out — exactly the queue from the last lesson. It's the one you want for **fairness and order**: print jobs, requests to a server, messages between programs, and the frontier of a breadth-first search.

A circular queue stores its items in a **fixed** number of slots and treats the last slot as if it were followed by the first one. The front and back indexes chase each other round the ring, so a slot freed by a dequeue is reused by a later enqueue — no item ever has to be shifted.

blocks.alt: Six slots. Slots 2, 3 and 4 hold 7, 8 and 9; front is at slot 2 and back at slot 4. Slots 0, 1 and 5 are free. An arrow from slot 5 curves back to slot 0: after the last slot comes the first one again.

blocks.text: Because its size is fixed, a circular queue can be **full** — then it must refuse new items, or overwrite the oldest one (a log that keeps only the last 1,000 lines does exactly that). Ring buffers sit under keyboard input, audio and video streaming and network cards. The **Array implementation** problem later in this course builds one step by step.

A **deque** (say "deck") lets you add and remove at **both** ends, all in O(1). Use only one end and it behaves like a stack; add at one end and remove at the other and it's a queue. That flexibility makes it the tool behind the **sliding window maximum**, undo histories with a size limit, and many breadth-first search tricks.

blocks.alt: A deque holding 3, 5, 8, 2. At the left end, items can be pushed onto the front or popped off it; at the right end, items can be pushed onto the back or popped off it. All four operations are O(1).

elements.text: in (green) and out (red) at both ends, all O(1)
elements.originalText: in (green) and out (red) at both ends, all O(1)

blocks.text: A classic use: is a word a **palindrome**? Put its letters in a deque, then keep taking one letter off the **front** and one off the **back**. If every pair matches, the word reads the same both ways.

blocks.caption: Each round takes one letter off each end of the deque.

blocks.text: A **priority queue** breaks the first-in, first-out rule on purpose: whoever has the **highest priority** — usually the smallest (or largest) key — leaves first, no matter when it arrived. Think of a hospital emergency room, where the most urgent patient is seen first.

blocks.alt: Three items arrive in the order 5, 1, 3. A priority queue that serves the smallest key first lets them leave in the order 1, 3, 5.

elements.text: not first in, first out: the smallest key always leaves first
elements.originalText: not first in, first out: the smallest key always leaves first

blocks.text: It's usually built on a **heap**, which inserts and removes in **O(log n)** and peeks in O(1). Priority queues power task schedulers, Dijkstra's shortest paths and "top k" questions — they get their own course, **Heap**.

items: **Simple queue** — join at the back, leave from the front: first in, first out.
**Circular queue** — the same on a fixed ring of slots; freed slots are reused, and it can be full.
**Deque** — add and remove at both ends in O(1); it can act as a stack or a queue.
**Priority queue** — the smallest (or largest) key leaves first, in O(log n) with a heap.
